Floor heating is the standard heat emitter in newer Danish dwellings. It is invisible, it frees wall space, and it potentially works with very low supply temperatures, which suits heat pumps and district heating very well.

Warm water from a manifold runs through a pipe loop in the floor of each room and returns a few kelvin cooler. The heat first warms the floor, and the floor surface then gives it to the room by radiation and convection (

In an older house with a large heat demand it gives good comfort, with warm feet and a small vertical temperature gradient.
A low-energy house is a different case. The heat loss is small,
only 10 W per m² of floor

at design conditions, and much less on an ordinary spring or autumn day. Solar and internal gains are large in comparison, and the heat that must be supplied is so small that it has to be delivered precisely. On a clear day in April a heating demand at night can turn into a surplus by noon. The heat emitter must therefore
: it must follow the demand closely, give less as soon as the gains rise, and nothing when they cover the loss.

A floor stores heat before it reaches the room, so its output follows the water with a delay. Water put into a heavy floor at 04:00 keeps warming the room after the sun has come out and the demand has gone. The heavier the floor, the longer the delay, and the harder it is to make the floor follow the demand.
This chapter judges how well, and when, floor heating suits low-energy houses. It uses four measures that apply to any heat emitter:
The heat delivered to the room. Heat that leaves through an open window must be paid for twice: once as heating energy, and again as discomfort.

The time integral of the difference between the room temperature and the setpoint, in K·h. Time below the setpoint is discomfort. Time above it is heat the room did not need, which usually leaves through an open window.

The return water goes back to the heat source. A low return temperature lets a heat pump run at a lower condensing temperature, and in district heating it reduces the heat loss of the return pipes. It is weighted by the mass flow, because the heat source sees the mixed return of all loops.

The peak hourly heat output divided by the mean output over the day. The heat source and the grid must be sized for the peak, and a heat pump runs most efficiently at a steady, low output. A ratio close to 1 means the emitter draws heat evenly.

The question for the designer is whether floor heating can meet these measures as well as a fast emitter, such as an electric panel radiator or air heating, which responds within minutes. The sections on build-up, time constant, hydronics and control explain the mechanisms.

Several elements delay the floor’s response when the heat demand of the room changes:
The room must first deviate from the setpoint before the controller reacts.
The wax must warm up or cool down before the valve moves. This gives a dead time of a few minutes and a stroke of a few minutes more.
At the low flow rates of floor heating the water takes several minutes to pass through a 100 m loop.
The floor must be charged or discharged before its surface temperature changes. This is by far the longest delay, from about an hour in a light floor to many hours in a heavy floor.
The first three add minutes to tens of minutes. Only the heat capacity of the floor is large enough to matter over a day, and the rest of this section is about that.

The two floors give different outputs with the same water temperature, because the resistance from the water to the room is smaller in the heavy floor (pipes cast in concrete, thin parquet) than in the light floor (pipes under 22 mm boards). To give the same output, the light floor needs warmer water.

The last two rows are the ones that matter in a low-energy house. When the heavy floor’s loop closes, the slab still holds about 500 Wh/m² more heat than at room temperature, and it hands this heat to the room over the next day. If the house needs 5 W/m² on average on a spring day, that is about four days’ heating stored in the floor. The room overheats, and the heat must be removed again by opening windows or by cooling.
A light floor holds 70 Wh/m², 14 % of that heat, and most of it is released within the first hour.
It follows the demand much better, but it still lags behind it, and the control loop adds more delay.

Extra: what would it take for the floor to follow the demand?

The lag is for the floor alone. The wax thermostat’s dead time and stroke, the room’s own heat capacity and the controller all add to it.
Several strategies reduce the problem, but none of them removes it:
With the supply only a few kelvin above the room, the floor delivers less when the room warms up, even with the valve open.
Heating stop and a broad deadband.
Stop heating above an outdoor temperature limit, for example 12–15 °C, and use a broad deadband between the heating and cooling setpoints, so the room temperature can float more.
Lower the setpoint in the morning on sunny days, using a weather forecast or model predictive control.
Remove the solar gain or the surplus heat (see Part D).
The same pipes can cool by 20–40 W/m², limited by the dew point and a minimum floor surface temperature of about 19–20 °C. But the floor is just as slow when cooling.

The conclusion is that a low-energy house needs a heat emitter that modulates with the demand: its output must follow a demand that is small and changes within minutes. A light floor with a time constant of about 1 hour nearly does. A heavy floor with a time constant of about 12 hours does not, whatever the control. A fast emitter, such as an electric panel radiator or air heating, follows the demand even more closely.

A heat pump or district heating. Floor heating needs a low supply temperature, typically 30–35 °C in a low-energy house, with 3–5 K between supply and return.

A circulation pump, a motorized two-way valve on the primary return and a bypass with a check valve. The more the two-way valve closes, the less water goes back to the heat source, and the more return water the pump draws through the bypass into the supply. This lowers the supply to the temperature set by the controller. The controller follows a heating curve, which raises the supply temperature as the outdoor temperature falls.

Distributes water to one loop per room, or several loops in large rooms. Each loop should be at most 80–100 m long to keep the pressure drop reasonable. Flow meters or balancing valves on the supply side set the design flow in each loop, so that every room gets its share (hydronic balancing).
Wax thermostats and room temperature sensors.

Each loop has a valve on the return side, opened and closed by a wax thermostat, an electrically heated wax actuator. The room temperature sensor switches it on and off, either directly or by pulse-width modulation (PWM). The valve only opens or closes the loop. It cannot change the water temperature.
A loop that gets too much flow returns water that is almost as warm as the supply. The temperature drop

The room with the short loop is heated fast and the room at the end of the long loop too slowly, and the usual response is to raise the supply temperature or the pump setting until the worst room is warm. Both make the other loops worse. A high return temperature lowers the efficiency of a heat pump, and in district heating it increases the heat loss of the return pipes and is often penalised in the tariff.
A high supply temperature gives a high return temperature

At a given flow, the difference between return and room temperature is a fixed fraction of the difference between supply and room temperature. A loop designed for 35/30 °C in a 20 °C room starts 15 K above the room and returns 10 K above it, a fraction of two thirds. Example: balancing floor heating with virtual sensors

studied the floor heating in an 85 m² apartment in a DGNB-Gold multi-family building in Copenhagen, built in 2017 (wall U = 0.12 W/(m²·K), windows 0.95 W/(m²·K)). District heating supplies risers that serve six apartments. In each apartment a mixing shunt with its own pump (Grundfos Alpha2 L 15-60, proportional pressure) lowers the supply to the floors. A motorized valve on the return controls the mixed supply temperature, and a check valve sits in the bypass, as in

. The kitchen/living room has two loops, the three bedrooms one each. Each loop has an on/off valve switched by the room thermostat. The floors are 14 mm wood on an 80 mm concrete slab with embedded pipes, over 93 mm insulation.

No flows or temperatures were measured in the loops. The apartment had only the data a modern installation already logs: the room temperatures and the valve status from the thermostats (1–5 min), the supply and return temperature and the flow from the apartment’s heat meter, and the current drawn by the pump (5 min), see

. The authors built a physical model of the installation in Modelica (Dymola), with the riser, the shunt, the pump curves, the manifold and one floor heating component per loop. Each pipe section and valve follows

. Nine parameters were unknown: the flow coefficient of each room loop, of the bypass and of the return valve, the riser pressure difference, the gain and setpoint of the shunt controller. A genetic algorithm (ModestPy) adjusted them until the model matched the measured return temperature, heat meter flow and pump current, by minimising the sum of their normalised RMS errors. The model was fitted on 14 days and validated on the following 17 days in January 2019.

Floor heating has two levels of control (

A wax thermostat is an on/off valve (

A wax thermostat is either open or closed
The wax thermostat cannot hold positions between fully open and fully closed. It is therefore controlled either on/off or with pulse-width modulation (PWM).

The loop opens when the room is below the setpoint minus a hysteresis and closes when it is above the setpoint plus the hysteresis. In this example the room needs more than 50 % output, and a proportional controller only gives more than 50 % when the room is below the setpoint. This remaining deviation is the offset. The I part of a PI controller removes it.

With PWM the room unit runs a P or PI controller and turns its output into a duty cycle for the wax thermostat. If 40 % output is required and the cycle is 15 min, the valve is only (fully) open for about 6 min of each cycle. On average this behaves like a valve that is 40 % open.

> - **PWM control.** The room unit runs a PI controller and turns its output into a duty cycle. With a 15–20 min cycle and 40 % output, the valve is open for about 6–8 min of each cycle. On average this behaves like a valve that is 40 % open.

shows how PWM works. The room unit compares the measured room temperature with a triangular signal that sweeps the proportional band once per cycle. The valve is open while the room is colder than the triangle. Below the band the valve stays open the whole cycle, and above the band it stays closed. Inside the band, the colder the room, the longer the valve is open in each cycle. The triangular signal plays the same role as the proportional band of a proportional controller: it sets how far the room must deviate before the valve is fully open or fully closed.

Self-regulation works best when the floor surface temperature is close to the room temperature, which requires a low supply temperature. With a high supply temperature the floor never cools, and a warmer room only trims its output a little. Self-regulation is also no substitute for control: in

A light floor uses about as much heat as the ideal heater: 11–14 % more with PI control, and 13 % less with the loop open at 23 °C.
Light floors perform closer to the ideal heater than heavy floors.

Across floor types, a low supply temperature carries through to a low return temperature, and especially in light floors self-regulation always gives a low return temperature. There are concerns, however: rooms may need different amounts of heat, because of their orientation and their internal gains.

Room control makes the load peaky: the peak hour is 5–14 times the daily mean, against about 2.5 for the ideal heater. PI control and the heating curve lower the ratio. Self-regulation gives the steadiest load, 1.5–1.9, because the floor takes heat whenever the room is cooler than the floor. The ratio is computed from hourly means, since a heat source serving many loops sees a smoother load than the PWM pulses of one loop.
A heavy floor does worse: it uses up to 57 % more heat and deviates up to 36 K·h more than the ideal heater, unless the supply temperature is kept low.

A light floor with PI control uses only 11–14 % more heat than an ideal heater. A heavy floor uses 22–35 % more, because heat stored at night comes out when the sun already heats the room.
In a heavy floor, keep the supply temperature low. The floor then limits its own output, and the room overheats less.

With PI control and the heating curve, floor heating returns the water 2–3.5 K above the setpoint, and with self-regulation only about 1.5 K, which suits a heat pump or district heating. On/off control at 40 °C supply loses this advantage in a light floor, with a return near 31 °C.
Room control makes the load peaky, 5–14 times the daily mean. A low, steady supply temperature without room control gives the steadiest load, below 2.

children.value: In buildings with several floors or apartments, one riser pump often feeds a manifold on each floor, each through its own shunt (

). The shunt pump circulates water through the floor loops. A thermostatic valve on the return limits the supply temperature: when the sensor bulb gets too warm, it throttles the water returned to the riser, so less hot water is drawn in and more return water is mixed back through the bypass. The check valve stops riser water from flowing backwards through the bypass into the return.

On each of two floors, a branch from the riser supply passes a bypass junction, a shunt pump and a sensor bulb before reaching a supply manifold with three connections. The return manifold has a wax thermostat on each connection. The return passes the bypass junction and a 2-way thermostatic valve, connected to the sensor bulb by a capillary, before rejoining the riser return. The bypass between return and supply has a check valve. One floor loop is drawn in full.

children.value: A riser with a riser pump feeding two floor heating manifolds, each through a shunt with its own pump, a 2-way thermostatic valve on the return and a check valve in the bypass. Three pumps in total. Only one floor loop per manifold is drawn.

The check valve in the bypass is spring loaded and needs a certain pressure difference to open. This becomes a problem in low-energy apartment buildings, where the floor loops need little heat but the riser pump keeps its pressure up (

). At design load the shunts draw a large flow from the riser, and the riser pump runs at its design point A. In mild weather the thermostatic valves throttle, the flow drawn from the riser becomes small, and a constant-speed riser pump runs up its curve to almost its shut-off head (point B). The riser pressure then pushes against the bypass. Before any water can flow up through the bypass, the thermostatic valve must absorb both the riser pressure and the opening pressure of the check valve. The valve ends up almost closed with a large pressure across it, so it hunts and can be noisy, and until the check valve opens the floor loops get either too little flow or water that is too hot.
A riser pump in proportional-pressure mode lowers its head as the flow falls (point C), which makes the problem much smaller. A check valve with a low opening pressure also helps.

Two system curves are shown, one for design and a steep one for low load. A dashed line 10 kPa above the constant-speed curve marks the pressure the thermostatic valve must absorb before the check valve opens.
